BORG

cross-validation for data that isn’t independent

BORG (Bounded Outcome Risk Guard) checks how a model is evaluated on spatial, temporal and grouped data: it tests whether observations depend on each other, builds cross-validation folds that keep dependent observations apart, and checks train/test splits for leakage, such as preprocessing fitted on the test rows.

Dependence is tested from the columns that carry structure: Moran’s I on the coordinates for spatial autocorrelation, the autocorrelation function and the Ljung-Box test on a time column, and the intraclass correlation for groups. The result is a diagnosis with a severity and a recommended fold scheme, and the folds are built from that scheme. When dependence is found, random k-fold cross-validation is switched off unless you request it, and the override is recorded in the result. You can then use the folds directly or compare them with random folds before deciding which estimate to report.

BORG supports:

  • Fold schemes for dependent data. borg_cv() builds spatial blocks, environmental blocks, checkerboard and hexagonal blocks, leave-location-out, buffered spatial folds, KNNDM folds matched to prediction points, chronological splits with an embargo, expanding and sliding windows, purged cross-validation, leave-group-out and spatial-temporal combinations.
  • Folds for modelling frameworks. The folds come as a list of train and test indices, or as objects for rsample, caret and mlr3.
  • Random against blocked cross-validation. borg_compare_cv() runs both on the same data and model and tests the difference with a paired t-test; borg_power() reports the effective sample size after blocking and the smallest effect still detectable.
  • Leakage checks. borg_inspect() checks splits and fitted objects for overlapping indices, duplicate rows (hash-based checks in C++), preprocessing fitted beyond the training rows, target leakage, group leakage and look-ahead in time.
  • Area of applicability. borg_aoa() and borg_di() mark prediction locations outside the predictor space of the training data, following Meyer and Pebesma (2021).
  • Methods text. summary() on a result writes a methods paragraph with the test statistics filled in, in APA, Nature or Ecology style, and borg_certificate() and borg_export() write the assessment as YAML or JSON.

The diagnostics follow evaluation principles described by Roberts et al. (2017), Kaufman et al. (2012), Kapoor and Narayanan (2023) and Linnenbrink et al. (2024), with the references in the DESCRIPTION. Risk Taxonomy lists each check, what it detects and how to fix it.

Installation

Install the released version from CRAN. Windows and macOS get a binary package and need no build tools:

install.packages("BORG")

The development version compiles C++ code. Install the build tools for your operating system first:

Operating system Build tools
Windows Rtools matching your R version
macOS Run xcode-select --install in Terminal
Debian / Ubuntu Install r-base-dev

Check that R can find the compiler:

pkgbuild::has_build_tools(debug = TRUE)

Then install BORG from GitHub:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/BORG")

BORG needs no system libraries beyond the compiler. Its C++ code links only to Rcpp, which is installed from CRAN with the package.

Usage

  1. Diagnose the data and build folds with borg().
  2. Compare random and blocked cross-validation with borg_compare_cv().
  3. Check an existing split or fitted preprocessing with borg_inspect().

The input is a data frame, an sf object or a terra SpatVector. coords names the two coordinate columns, time the time column and groups the grouping column; target names the response. With an sf or SpatVector input the coordinates are taken from the geometry.

library(BORG)

set.seed(1)
n <- 200
d <- data.frame(lon = runif(n, 0, 20), lat = runif(n, 0, 20))
d$response <- sin(d$lon / 3) + cos(d$lat / 3) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)

result <- borg(d, coords = c("lon", "lat"), target = "response")
result
#> BORG Result
#> ===========
#> 
#> Dependency:  SPATIAL (moderate severity)
#> Strategy:    spatial_block
#> Folds:       5
#> 
#> Random CV would inflate metrics by ~8%
#> 
#> Fold sizes:  train 148-174, test 26-52
#> 
#> Access components:
#>   $diagnosis  - BorgDiagnosis object
#>   $folds      - List of train/test index vectors
#>   $cv         - Full borg_cv object

The response varies smoothly in space, so the diagnosis finds spatial autocorrelation and builds five spatial blocks instead of random folds.

borg_compare_cv() fits the same model on random and on blocked folds and reports the gap:

cmp <- borg_compare_cv(
  d,
  formula = response ~ lon + lat,
  coords = c("lon", "lat"),
  repeats = 5,
  seed = 1,
  verbose = FALSE
)
cmp
#> CV Comparison Results
#> =====================
#> 
#> Metric: rmse
#> Random CV:  0.8806 (SD: 0.0040)
#> Blocked CV: 1.2735 (SD: 0.0000)
#> 
#> Inflation: 30.8% deflated***
#> p-value: 2.522e-09 (paired t-test, n=5 repeats)
#> 
#> Random CV significantly deflates rmse estimates.

summary() turns the diagnosis into a paragraph for the methods section:

summary(result)
#> 
#> Spatial autocorrelation was detected in the data (Moran's I = 0.29, p < 0.001) with an estimated autocorrelation range of 10.9 units. Model performance was evaluated using spatial block cross-validation (k = 5 folds). Random cross-validation was avoided as it would be expected to inflate performance estimates by approximately 8%. Cross-validation strategy was determined using the BORG package (version 0.3.2) for R.

Fold schemes and modelling frameworks

borg() chooses the scheme from the diagnosis, and borg_cv() takes a scheme by name through strategy. output = "rsample" returns folds that tidymodels functions accept:

folds <- borg(d, coords = c("lon", "lat"), target = "response",
              output = "rsample")

Spatial Cross-Validation and Temporal Cross-Validation go through each scheme, and Framework Integration covers caret, mlr3, ENMeval and biomod2.

Checking a split for leakage

With train_idx and test_idx, borg() and borg_inspect() check an existing split. Passed a fitted preprocessing object and the data, borg_inspect() checks whether its parameters were estimated on rows beyond the training set. Here a principal component analysis was fitted on all rows:

x <- iris[, 1:4]
pca <- prcomp(x, scale. = TRUE)
borg_inspect(pca, train_idx = 1:100, test_idx = 101:150, data = x)
#> BorgRisk Assessment
#> ===================
#> 
#> Status: INVALID (3 hard violations) — Resistance is futile
#>   Hard violations:  3
#>   Soft inflations:  0
#>   Train indices:    100 rows
#>   Test indices:     50 rows
#>   Inspected at:     2026-10-23 01:28:36
#> 
#> --- HARD VIOLATIONS (must fix) ---
#> 
#> [1] preprocessing_leak
#>     PCA centering was computed on data beyond training set (mean difference: 0.897)
#>     Source: prcomp
#>     Affected: 50 indices (first 5: 101, 102, 103, 104, 105)
#>     Fix: Refit preprocessing on training data only. Auto-fix: borg_assimilate(workflow)
#> 
#> [2] preprocessing_leak
#>     PCA scaling was computed on data beyond training set (sd difference: 0.31575)
#>     Source: prcomp
#>     Affected: 50 indices (first 5: 101, 102, 103, 104, 105)
#>     Fix: Refit preprocessing on training data only. Auto-fix: borg_assimilate(workflow)
#> 
#> [3] preprocessing_leak
#>     PCA loadings were computed on data beyond training set (max loading difference: 0.1729)
#>     Source: prcomp
#>     Affected: 50 indices (first 5: 101, 102, 103, 104, 105)
#>     Fix: Refit preprocessing on training data only. Auto-fix: borg_assimilate(workflow)

Hard violations (overlap, duplicates, preprocessing leakage, target leakage, group leakage, look-ahead) mark the evaluation invalid. Soft inflations, such as a predictor close to the threshold for target leakage or test points close to training points, give a warning and are recorded.

Area of applicability and prediction maps

borg_aoa() and borg_di() compute the dissimilarity index and the area of applicability of Meyer and Pebesma (2021) for prediction locations. borg_extract(), borg_thin(), borg_predict_raster() and borg_leaflet() cover raster extraction, spatial thinning, prediction maps and an interactive map of the folds. Area of Applicability and Extrapolation Detection shows them on simulated data.

Documentation

Start with Quick Start: simulated data with known dependence, from the diagnosis to folds, leakage checks and the comparison of random and blocked cross-validation.

  • Spatial Cross-Validation: spatial blocks, block size optimization, environmental blocking, buffered folds and KNNDM.
  • Temporal Cross-Validation: temporal blocks, expanding windows, embargo periods and concept drift.
  • Risk Taxonomy: each leakage check, what it detects and how to fix it.
  • Framework Integration: folds for tidymodels, caret, mlr3, ENMeval and biomod2.
  • Model Comparison with Blocked Cross-Validation: the inflation from random folds, model ranking, confidence intervals and null tests.
  • Feature Selection with Blocked Cross-Validation: block-permutation importance and forward selection.
  • Area of Applicability and Extrapolation Detection: where predictions leave the training data.
  • Post-Fit Diagnostics: residual structure, calibration, null tests, conformal prediction and bootstrap uncertainty.
  • Full reference: every function.

Getting help

Questions and bug reports go to the GitHub issues. A bug report is easiest to act on with a small reproducible example, for instance made with reprex.
